learn.b: A database stores data in tables, like spreadsheets. Each row is one thing, like one student, and each column is one fact about it, like the name. A query is a question you ask the database, and SQL is the language you write it in.
SELECT lists the columns you want and FROM says which table they come from. Separate several columns with commas. A semicolon at the end finishes the statement.
learn.code:
SELECT name, city
FROM students;

learn.b: SELECT * means all columns. AS gives a column a nicer name in the result. DISTINCT removes repeated rows so each value shows once.

A table does not promise any order unless you ask for one. Adding ORDER BY id at the end gives a fixed order, and a later unit teaches it fully. In the challenges, always add ORDER BY when you get several rows.
learn.code:
SELECT name FROM students
ORDER BY id;

qs.q: Which keyword chooses the columns to show?

What does this query return?
In a table, each column is one fact about the things stored, like a name.
qs.why: Columns are fields, rows are records.

learn.b: WHERE keeps only the rows where a condition is true. It goes after FROM. Without it, the query returns every row.
SQL compares with = for equal, <> or != for not equal, and < > <= >=. Notice that a single = is used for comparing here. You can compare numbers and text.
Text values go inside single quotes, like 'Rome'. Numbers have no quotes. Double quotes are for column names, so use single quotes for text.
learn.code:
SELECT * FROM students
WHERE grade = 10;

learn.b: A missing value is called NULL. You cannot check it with =. You must write IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.
learn.code:

learn.b: ORDER BY sorts the result by a column. The default is ascending, from small to large or A to Z. Add DESC for the other way.
You can sort by more than one column, separated by commas. The second column breaks ties in the first. Each column can have its own ASC or DESC.
learn.code:
SELECT title, rating FROM games
ORDER BY rating DESC, title ASC;

learn.b: LIMIT keeps only the first rows of the result. Together with ORDER BY it finds the top or bottom items, like the 3 best rated games. It always goes at the very end.
OFFSET skips rows before LIMIT starts counting. It is used for pages: LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3 gives rows four to six. Always sort first so the pages are stable.

learn.b: An aggregate function turns many rows into one value. The result is a single row. The common ones are COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX.
learn.code: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students;

learn.b: COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(column) counts rows where that column is not NULL. Add WHERE first to count only some rows.
SUM adds up a number column. AVG gives the average and may have decimals. Both skip NULL values.
learn.code:
SELECT SUM(qty) FROM orders;
SELECT AVG(price) FROM games;

learn.b: MIN gives the smallest value and MAX the largest. They work on numbers and also on text. You can do math with the results.
learn.code:
SELECT MAX(price) - MIN(price)
FROM games;

learn.b: GROUP BY splits rows into groups with the same value, and an aggregate runs once for each group. For example, one count per genre. Every column in SELECT must be in GROUP BY or be inside an aggregate.
Put SUM, AVG or others next to the group column to get totals per group. The result has one row per group. Add ORDER BY to fix the order.
learn.code:
SELECT customer, SUM(qty)
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer
ORDER BY customer;

learn.b: WHERE filters rows before they are grouped. HAVING filters the groups after the aggregates are calculated. So a test like SUM(qty) > 3 must go in HAVING.
learn.code:
SELECT customer, SUM(qty)
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer
HAVING SUM(qty) > 3;

learn.b: A query can use both. WHERE removes rows first, then GROUP BY makes groups, then HAVING removes groups. The clause order is fixed: WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY.
learn.code:
SELECT product, COUNT(*)
FROM orders
WHERE qty >= 1
GROUP BY product
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;

learn.b: Real databases split data across tables. Here students holds names and scores holds points, linked by student_id. A JOIN puts matching rows together in one result.
INNER JOIN keeps only rows that have a match in both tables. ON says which columns must be equal. Name columns with the table name, like students.id, when both tables have a column of that name.
learn.code:
SELECT students.name, scores.points
FROM students
INNER JOIN scores
  ON students.id = scores.student_id;

learn.b: A short alias after the table name saves typing. Then you write s.name instead of students.name. The alias works everywhere in the query.
After joining, you can use WHERE, GROUP BY and aggregates as usual. Students with no match do not appear in an INNER JOIN. Plain JOIN means INNER JOIN.
learn.code:
SELECT s.name, SUM(sc.points)
FROM students s
JOIN scores sc ON s.id = sc.student_id
GROUP BY s.name;

qs.q: Which clause says how two tables match?
What does INNER JOIN keep?
o: Only rows with a match in both tables
All rows of the first table

learn.b: A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table, the one in FROM, even when it has no match. The columns of the right table are NULL for those rows. Use it when you must not lose rows.
learn.code:
SELECT s.name, sc.points
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN scores sc
  ON s.id = sc.student_id;

learn.b: Count a column of the right table, not COUNT(*). COUNT(sc.id) skips NULL, so a student with no scores gets 0. COUNT(*) would give 1 for them.
learn.code:
SELECT s.name, COUNT(sc.id)
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN scores sc ON s.id = sc.student_id
GROUP BY s.name;

learn.b: To find rows with no match, LEFT JOIN and then keep rows where the right side is NULL. This answers questions like which students have no scores. Use IS NULL for this test.
learn.code:
SELECT s.name
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN scores sc ON s.id = sc.student_id
WHERE sc.id IS NULL;

learn.b: LEFT JOIN depends on which table is on the left. Swapping the tables changes which rows are kept. A RIGHT JOIN does the opposite, but SQLite works well with LEFT JOIN, so write the main table first.

qs.q: What does LEFT JOIN keep?

learn.b: A subquery is a SELECT inside brackets, used inside another query. The inner query runs first and its result is used by the outer query. This lets you compare with a value you do not know in advance.
If the subquery returns one value, use it with a comparison. For example, games that cost more than the average price. The brackets are required.
If the subquery returns a column of values, use IN. The outer query keeps rows whose value is in that list. NOT IN keeps those that are not.
A common pattern is comparing with MAX or MIN. This finds all rows with the best value, even if there is a tie. It is safer than LIMIT 1 for ties.

learn.b: CREATE TABLE makes a new table. You list each column with a name and a data type. Common types are INTEGER for whole numbers, TEXT for text and REAL for decimals.
A primary key is a column that identifies each row, so no two rows share the same value. It is usually an id. Mark it with PRIMARY KEY.
Constraints are rules the database checks. NOT NULL means a value is required. UNIQUE means no repeats. DEFAULT gives a value when you do not provide one. CHECK tests a condition.

A foreign key is a column that points to the primary key of another table. It links the tables and stops you from pointing to a row that does not exist. It is how scores.student_id is linked to students.id.

learn.b: An index is like the index of a book. It helps the database find rows fast without reading the whole table. Indexes make reading faster but make writing a little slower, so use them on columns you search often.
learn.code:
CREATE INDEX idx_games_genre
ON games (genre);

learn.b: Normalization means organising tables so each fact is stored once. If a city name is copied in many rows, you can get typos and updates become hard. Split the data into tables and link them with keys.

First normal form: each cell holds one value, not a list. Second: every column depends on the whole key. Third: columns do not depend on other non-key columns. The practical idea is one fact, one place.
A view is a saved query that acts like a table. It does not store a copy of the data, it runs the query each time. Views make complex queries simple and can hide columns.

qs.q: What does an index do?
What is the main idea of normalization?
qs.why: Each fact lives in one place.

lab.q: Challenge: create a view cheap_games with titles of games priced below 6. The SELECT is written for you.
lab.setup:
CREATE TABLE games (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT, genre TEXT, price INTEGER, rating INTEGER);
INSERT INTO games VALUES (1,'Space Run','arcade',5,8),(2,'Cube Farm','sim',10,7),(3,'Dino Dash','arcade',3,9),(4,'Sky Racer','racing',8,6),(5,'Pixel Quest','rpg',12,9),(6,'Block Tag','arcade',0,5),(7,'Turbo Kart','racing',7,8);
lab.starter:
-- write the CREATE VIEW first
SELECT title FROM cheap_games ORDER BY title;

tests.expect:
Block Tag
Dino Dash
Space Run

lab.hint: CREATE VIEW cheap_games AS SELECT title FROM games WHERE price < 6;
lab.solution:
CREATE VIEW cheap_games AS SELECT title FROM games WHERE price < 6;
SELECT title FROM cheap_games ORDER BY title;
lab.why: A view is used just like a table.

lab.q: Challenge: create an index named idx_games_genre on the genre column of games. The check query is written for you.
lab.setup:
CREATE TABLE games (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT, genre TEXT, price INTEGER, rating INTEGER);
INSERT INTO games VALUES (1,'Space Run','arcade',5,8),(2,'Cube Farm','sim',10,7),(3,'Dino Dash','arcade',3,9),(4,'Sky Racer','racing',8,6),(5,'Pixel Quest','rpg',12,9),(6,'Block Tag','arcade',0,5),(7,'Turbo Kart','racing',7,8);
lab.starter:
-- write the CREATE INDEX first
SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'index' AND name = 'idx_games_genre';
lab.solution:
CREATE INDEX idx_games_genre ON games (genre);
SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'index' AND name = 'idx_games_genre';
lab.why: The database lists its indexes in sqlite_master.
